To poise means to hold something — or yourself — in a carefully balanced, still position, usually right before taking action.

Think of a diver standing at the edge of a board: body completely under control, perfectly still, not yet moving but entirely ready. That moment of deliberate, suspended balance is exactly what this word captures.

When you poise something, you hold it in careful balance at a specific position — almost always just before doing something with it.

  • She poised the pen above the paper before signing her name. (Held it hovering, balanced, right at the moment of readiness.)
  • He poised the ball on his fingertips. (Held it in steady, deliberate balance.)
  • The hawk poised in mid-air before diving for its prey. (Hung perfectly still, suspended, right before action.)

Notice the key quality here: it isn't just balancing. It's balancing with intention and stillness, right at the edge of doing something. There's a sense of controlled tension — like a coiled spring, or a breath held in.
"Poised" — the form you'll see most often

In everyday language, you'll encounter this verb most commonly as poised (past participle), and it carries the same core meaning: balanced, still, and ready — right at the edge of action.

  • She stood poised at the top of the stairs. (Perfectly balanced, still, ready to move.)
  • The cat crouched poised before the mouse. (Absolutely still, in perfect balance, about to pounce.)
  • He sat poised at the keyboard, waiting for the signal. (Held himself in a state of controlled readiness.)
"Poised to do something" — the figurative use

This is where the word expands beyond the physical, and it's extremely common in writing and journalism.

When someone or something is poised to do something, it means they are positioned, ready, and very likely to do it — right on the verge of it happening.

  • She is poised to become the youngest CEO in the company's history. (She's in exactly the right position; it's about to happen.)
  • The country was poised to enter a new era of prosperity. (Right at the threshold; the change was coming.)
  • He was poised to win the championship before his injury. (He was in a perfect, ready, favorable position — until something changed it.)

The figurative meaning preserves the same feeling as the physical one: something is suspended at a critical moment, right between the present and what's about to unfold.

Poise implies something more than just "balance" or "ready." It carries a quality of composure and deliberateness. Something poised is not frantic, not accidental, not rushed. It is controlled, calm, and intentional. The word quietly suggests that whatever comes next will be purposeful.

Compare it to similar words:

  • Balance just means not falling. Poise adds intentionality and readiness for action.
  • Prepare means getting ready over a span of time. Poise is about being at that moment of readiness — right on the edge.
  • Hover is about being suspended in air. Poise is broader: you can poise a pen, poise yourself on a ledge, or poise a company for growth.
A few more examples to lock it in

• The surgeon poised the scalpel above the patient's skin. (Held it in precise, controlled balance before cutting.)
  • She poised herself on the narrow ledge, arms outstretched. (Carefully balanced herself, staying composed and still.)
  • He poised his hand over the letter, hesitating to sign. (Hand hovering, suspended at a moment of decision.)
  • The startup is poised for explosive growth. (In a favorable, ready position — growth is coming.)
  • The troops were poised to advance at dawn. (Positioned, ready, waiting for the moment to act.)

In one sentence: To poise is to hold something (or yourself) in a state of deliberate, controlled balance — suspended, still, and ready — right at the threshold of action.
